overview: This 30-page Department of State “List of Papers” register summarizes correspondence filed under 894.6363 concerning petroleum policy in Japan and Japanese-controlled Manchuria from April 1933 through January 1935. It traces proposals for a state oil monopoly, enactment and implementation of Japan’s Petroleum Industry Control Law, import licensing, storage requirements, sales quotas, Soviet competition, oil-security concerns, and the threatened exclusion or restriction of foreign firms—especially Socony-Vacuum/Standard-Vacuum and Rising Sun/Shell. The entries also document intensive consultation among American oil executives, the State Department, the U.S. embassies in Tokyo and London, and British and Dutch diplomats over coordinated representations to Japan, alongside the closely related creation of a Manchukuo petroleum monopoly. These pages are an archival register rather than the full texts of the listed papers; several entries are cross-references, and pages 23–24 are garbled duplicate versions of the same index sheet.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: initial reports on Japan’s oil problem, items 32–33
subfiles.about: Registers an April despatch and May telegram on proposed Japanese control of petroleum and the danger to foreign companies.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records Grew’s despatch on attempts to displace Socony-Vacuum and Rising Sun and redirect Japanese oil purchases from the United States to Russia. It also lists a telegram on proposals for a government monopoly or licensing system and the reactions of the British and Dutch embassies.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: foreign oil interests and the London conference, items 34–40
subfiles.about: Indexes May–June correspondence on threats to American oil interests and possible international discussions in London.
subfiles.summary: Entries cover Standard Oil’s review of adverse Japanese developments, Grew’s reports for possible use at the London Economic Conference, and British and Dutch diplomatic representations. They also record information on Manchurian schemes, correspondence with oil companies, and a proposal to convene Japanese and foreign oil representatives in London.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Socony-Vacuum consultations and proposed London meeting, items 41–46
subfiles.about: Registers corporate correspondence and State Department memoranda about organizing foreign oil interests and responding to Japanese control plans.
subfiles.summary: Socony-Vacuum thanked the Department for its assistance and suggested that company representatives meet in London before approaching national delegations. The page also notes Henry Dundas’s expected visit, Japanese plans for control of the oil trade, a Salisbury memorandum on multinational coordination, and inquiries about the Department’s response to possible nationalization.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Japanese and Manchurian petroleum policy, items 47–53
subfiles.about: Indexes reports on emerging Japanese and Manchukuo petroleum policies, Russian imports, and licensing proposals.
subfiles.summary: The entries describe correspondence about a new Manchurian company, rivalry between the Japanese military and the South Manchuria Railway, and developments considered unfavorable to Socony-Vacuum. They also cover Russian oil shipments, anticipated licensing of oil companies, a Commerce Department account of Japan’s national oil policy, and Matsukata’s entry into the gasoline market.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: movement toward the Petroleum Control Law, items 54–60
subfiles.about: Registers late-1933 and early-1934 papers on proposed petroleum controls, Soviet gasoline, and diplomatic responses to the bill submitted to the Diet.
subfiles.summary: The sheet notes discussion of a solution modeled on the French system, continued disruption by Soviet gasoline, and a conversation with Socony-Vacuum manager J. C. Goold. March 1934 entries cover the government control bill, British representations, instructions for an American approach, the law’s passage by the Diet, and Dooman’s recommendations.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: implementation and international reaction, items 61–67
subfiles.about: Indexes reports on enactment and enforcement of Japan’s Petroleum Industry Control Law and its expected effects on foreign firms.
subfiles.summary: Grew reported representations to the vice minister and the promulgation of the control measure, while other entries summarize probable provisions, Romanian barter proposals, and a Soviet-related gasoline war. Later telegrams concern enforcement, consultations with Standard Oil executives, and British proposals for coordinated corporate and governmental resistance.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: gasoline quotas, storage, and diplomatic coordination, items 68–71
subfiles.about: Registers August–September papers about Standard-Vacuum’s quota, storage requirements, and British-American consultation.
subfiles.summary: Standard-Vacuum reported the gasoline-sales quota assigned for the second half of 1934 and supplied a memorandum of foreign-company complaints. Telegrams exchanged with London and Tokyo reviewed the Petroleum Industry Law, while Grew linked Japan’s storage requirements to the strategic value of its merchant fleet and forwarded company protests.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: British, Dutch, and corporate approaches, items 72–77
subfiles.about: Summarizes September discussions among Hornbeck, Teagle, Dutch diplomats, and British officials concerning protests against the petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: The badly formatted sheet records British communication with the Foreign Office and B. Kleijn Molekamp’s warning that Dutch interests exceeded the affected American interests. It also summarizes repeated Teagle-Hornbeck telephone conversations, a Dutch aide-mémoire, and British encouragement for the American ambassador in Tokyo to make parallel representations.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: formal informal representations, items 78–79
subfiles.about: Registers instructions and reports concerning oral American representations to Japan in September 1934.
subfiles.summary: The United States instructed Grew to express hope that American petroleum interests would be spared unusual hazards and burdensome restrictions under Law No. 26. Grew subsequently read the message to the Japanese foreign minister, who promised that the competent authorities would consider the foreign companies’ position; London was informed confidentially.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: skeletal register entries 80–86
subfiles.about: Provides a partly lost or illegible register of diplomatic and departmental papers concerning the Japanese petroleum question.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text identifies Neville despatches and telegrams, a communication from Great Britain, and papers by Millard, Hornbeck, and Teagle dated from August through October 1934. The OCR preserves no substantive abstracts for these entries, so their precise contents cannot be recovered from this page.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Hornbeck memoranda on coordinated action, items 87–93
subfiles.about: Indexes internal memoranda recording State Department discussions with American, British, and Dutch participants.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck briefed Secretary Ickes before a meeting with Deterding and Teagle, after which the oil executives and officials discussed remedial action against Japanese controls. Further memoranda record requests from Molekamp, several Teagle-Hornbeck conversations, uncertainty over British initiative, and consideration of foreign control of export markets.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: petroleum-law consultations and military intelligence, items 94–99
subfiles.about: Registers September–October discussions with oil executives and Dutch diplomats, a War Department report, and company objections to storage rules.
subfiles.summary: Teagle and Chester O. Swain gave Hornbeck a comprehensive memorandum, while Hamilton informed Molekamp about American instructions for informal representations. Other entries describe a wide-ranging petroleum discussion, military intelligence on Japanese oil purchases, and Standard-Vacuum cables emphasizing the law’s storage provisions and official reporting forms.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: approaching crisis under the petroleum law, items 100–106
subfiles.about: Indexes October–November reports that foreign companies faced an imminent crisis over import and storage plans.
subfiles.summary: Grew warned that the companies could not comply with immediate Japanese demands and suggested deciding American policy before the Petroleum Committee met. The page also records a detailed Neville report, company cables from Yokohama, a military-attaché report, Hornbeck’s conversation with Teagle, Japan’s informal reply to earlier representations, and Parker’s request for clarification.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: British aide-mémoire and search for joint action, items 107–112
subfiles.about: Registers late-October and early-November discussions about coordinated representations on Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmitted a British aide-mémoire, a Japanese letter to Standard-Vacuum, and a Dickover-Kurusu conversation. Teagle and Hornbeck then exchanged cables and telephone views about joint action, with Hornbeck repeatedly arguing that the first governmental initiative should come from Britain and the Netherlands while the companies devised a common program.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: company cables and mounting pressure, items 113–117
subfiles.about: Indexes company communications and diplomatic reports about Japanese demands for data and a possible united foreign front.
subfiles.summary: Standard-Vacuum forwarded a Yokohama cable, while Norman H. Davis supplied a Baltimore Sun article and the Mukden post transmitted a related despatch. Grew reported the Dutch minister’s call for unity among the companies and three governments, relayed a coded company message, and described the November 15 deadline for submitting information on Form No. 4.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: embargo discussion and company mission to Japan, items 118–122
subfiles.about: Registers Hornbeck’s conversations about possible restrictions on oil exports and the planned arrival of foreign-company representatives in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Parker and Hornbeck discussed a reported refusal to supply crude oil and the prospect of coordinated governmental representations. Parker then asked whether the United States might impose an embargo or restriction, while Teagle discussed British inaction, Dutch East Indian trade, and precautions against excessive company commitments; Grew also noted the law’s continuing difficulties.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: waiting for British action, items 123–127
subfiles.about: Indexes November memoranda and correspondence on British intentions, Manchukuo, and the Japanese reply to American representations.
subfiles.summary: The Department cautioned Parker about Japan’s reserved power to control prices. Mackay and Hornbeck recorded discussions with Teagle and Coe about anticipated British action, London naval talks, and the Japanese and Manchukuo monopolies; Grew transmitted the Foreign Office’s October 31 reply, and Coe forwarded Orville Harden’s report from London.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: British-American friction and information exchange, items 128–131
subfiles.about: Registers discussions of filing extensions, British dissatisfaction, and the scope of planned company negotiations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Teagle reported Shell’s decision to seek more time for submitting required information. Phillips explained to the British ambassador why Washington expected Britain to assume greater responsibility, while Hornbeck discussed the planned company delegation with Coe and responded cautiously to Wiggin’s request for information on Japan and Manchuria.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Japanese proposal for a commercial compromise, items 132–135
subfiles.about: Indexes reports that Japanese officials sought nominal company compliance while moving the dispute from diplomatic to commercial channels.
subfiles.summary: Grew relayed the Standard-Vacuum manager’s view that a compromise proposed by the commerce vice minister might permit nominal compliance without foreclosing further diplomacy. Other telegrams describe the ministry’s ultimatum on import and storage plans and the November 20 conference at which Japanese authorities appeared more reasonable but sought to privatize the dispute.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: British willingness for concerted action, items 136–139
subfiles.about: Registers company plans and a London report that British officials favored concerted action by British and American oil interests.
subfiles.summary: Coe described British Foreign Office deliberations and the proposed travels of Parker and Walden to Tokyo and possibly Hsinking. Bingham reported Dooman and Millard’s conversation with Orde, who emphasized the unified position of British oil interests, while Teagle supplied a Deterding cable and Coe compared the French and Japanese petroleum laws.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: renewed representations and visiting executives, items 140–143
subfiles.about: Indexes late-November and early-December discussions on compromise, diplomatic representations, and visits by senior oil-company representatives.
subfiles.summary: The Department raised no objection to a company compromise supported by the firms and both embassies, while reporting that Grew had been told to deliver a firmly worded aide-mémoire. Grew submitted a report with enclosures, and Coe described plans for Godber, Walden, and Parker to visit Japan and quoted Hashimoto’s defense of the law’s stockholding requirement.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: tripartite consultation and British policy, item 144 and related papers
subfiles.about: Registers acknowledgments, enclosures, and diplomatic exchanges aimed at closer American-British-Dutch cooperation.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledged papers from Teagle and Coe, including Deterding’s cable and a comparison of French and Japanese law, and noted renewed American representations on the Manchukuo monopoly. Instructions to London called for a full exchange among the three governments and the oil interests, while Bingham reported the British position after Dooman and Millard met Orde and Mandell.

subfiles.title: Garbled duplicate List of Papers sheet, items 145–148
subfiles.about: A severely corrupted duplicate index page covering diplomatic discussion of the Japanese and Manchukuo petroleum problems.
subfiles.summary: The legible portions identify a State Department memorandum, Grew’s December 8 telegram, and cross-references to reports on the Petroleum Industry Law and Manchurian monopoly. Its contents substantially duplicate the clearer register sheet on page 24.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Lindsay conversation and renewed Anglo-American démarche, items 145–148
subfiles.about: Indexes a conversation with the British ambassador and Grew’s report on proposed parallel American and British representations.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck and British Ambassador Lindsay discussed confusion caused by British Foreign Office inquiries and press claims that Japan might mediate between British and American oil interests. Grew then reported that Clive had prepared a provisional aide-mémoire but was instructed to act only if the American ambassador made a similar approach; two additional entries are cross-references.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: disagreement over a further démarche, items 149–150
subfiles.about: Registers December exchanges between Washington, London, and Tokyo over the timing and form of renewed representations.
subfiles.summary: The Department questioned why the British Foreign Office favored a further démarche and instructed that Dooman should cease appearing in the matter outside the embassy. Bingham replied that Clive’s proposed action was only another informal representation, while Grew reported Kurusu’s suggestion that foreign and Japanese oil companies unite in protest and recommended further action.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: consultations on a common British-American position, items 151–154
subfiles.about: Indexes efforts to reconcile British and American policy and prepare for talks between oil executives and Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: Atherton confirmed communication with the British Foreign Office, and Coe forwarded notes of a Yoshino-Kurusu interview with Goold and Ely. Washington delayed action while consulting London, asked the Foreign Office to formulate a tentative common understanding, and received a report on British preferences for prospective high-level oil discussions.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: authorization for joint action, items 155–156
subfiles.about: Registers instructions allowing parallel British-American action and consultation with local oil-company representatives.
subfiles.summary: Washington advised Grew to consult Clive and, if all parties agreed, proceed along the lines discussed with London. Grew replied that both embassies would first confer jointly with the companies because Japan’s oral response might not reveal whether the government would remain adamant, and he separately transmitted a company message to Shanghai.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: preparations for company talks in Japan, items 157–160
subfiles.about: Indexes preparations for special oil-company representatives to travel from Shanghai to Japan and the embassies’ December 27 representations.
subfiles.summary: Coe expected the Shanghai representatives to proceed to Japan once the governmental position had been clarified. Additional entries cover American assurances that policy remained unchanged after the London Naval Conversation, records of British Foreign Office discussions, sympathetic reception of parallel embassy representations by Kurusu, and Grew’s report on American oil interests.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: announcement of representations and arrival of delegates, items 161–163
subfiles.about: Registers the public disclosure of the American representations and arrangements for Standard-Vacuum and British representatives to negotiate in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew reported Japanese press coverage of the American démarche and Kurusu’s statement that Commerce and Industry officials would receive the company representatives. Correspondence clarified Washington’s unchanged position, corrected misunderstandings held by Walden and Parker, and announced that Walden, Parker, and Goold had arrived from Shanghai for talks expected in early January 1935.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: joint company conferences and use of diplomatic codes, items 164–165
subfiles.about: Indexes final preparations for united British-American company negotiations and a request to transmit private messages in official diplomatic code.
subfiles.summary: Coe reported that misunderstandings had been cleared up and that Walden and Parker were traveling from Shanghai to Yokohama. Washington favored joint British-American conferences with Japanese officials, while Grew sought instructions after the representatives requested use of the State Department code for sensitive commercial messages during talks beginning January 9.

interest: The register offers an unusually detailed chronology of how Japanese economic regulation, imperial policy in Manchukuo, and strategic concern over petroleum supplies became intertwined. It is especially useful for studying the close but sometimes uneasy relationship between multinational oil companies and the American, British, and Dutch governments: corporate executives repeatedly supplied intelligence, pressed for diplomatic action, and coordinated their negotiating positions with officials. The abstracts also expose friction within the proposed foreign coalition, including Washington’s insistence that Britain take the initiative and British frustration at that position. As an archival finding aid, the document can guide historians to missing or dispersed telegrams, memoranda, company enclosures, military reports, and related Manchurian files despite the OCR corruption and duplicated index sheet.
